full_judgment:
This rule was issued calling upon the Deputy Commissioner, Jessore and opposite patty No; 2 to show cause as to why the order dated 18.3.78 passed by the Additional Sessions Judge,  Jessore  in Criminal Motion No. 181 of 1976 directing further enquiry in C.R. Case No.  286C of 1976 dismissed under section 203 by the Magistrate Magura on 24. 11.76 should not be set-aside. 

 2. This Rule arises out of an application filed by Rustom Ali on 3.5.73 to. the then Prime Mnister alleging that on 13.1.73 at 4 about  P.M. four persons were kidnapped by the Petitioners from Sobuj Sanga Club of Noahata Union, under Moharnmadpur P.S. Jessore and another person was taken on the next day at 10 a.m. for interrogation by petitioner No. 14. All these five persons were untraced and as they were killed, whereupon the then Prime Minister directed the Officer-in-Charge Mohammadpur P.S. directing that the application be treated as an  F.I.R. Then the police investigated into the matter and submitted final report on 12.2.74 and the said final report was accepted by the Sub divisional Magistrate, Magura on 13.3.74 and all the accused persons were discharged. Thereafter a naraji petition was filed by the complainant Syed Rustom Ali on 29.3.74 before the Sub-divisional Magistrate, Magura against the final report who sent the petition to the Officer-in-charge Mohammadpur for enquiry and report. The complainant without waiting for the report filed another petition of com-plaint on 14.5.74 to the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Magura, regarding the same incident whereupon the learned Magistrate examined the complainant on oath and transferred the case to another Magistrate for holding Judicial enquiry into the matter. When the judicial enquiry was being held the complainant was found absent consecutively for two days i.e. on 30.5.74 and 6.6.74 whereupon the learned Magistrate ordered the case to be filed. Thereafter the complainant filed another petition for revival of the petition for Judicial enquiry and the same was revived and three witnesses were examined on 1.7.74 and time was allowed for examination of further witnesses but on 4, 11.74 the complainant filed a petition stating that he was not willing to continue the proceedings as the witnesses were not willing to depose in the case. As such the learned Magistrate dropped the Judicial enquiry and complainant's petition was dismissed on 4.11.74. The complainant thereafter on 24.6.76 filed another petition of complaint before the Sub divisional Magistrate, Magura whereupon the complainant was examined on oath and the matter remained pending for about 5 months till 24.11.76 for want of original case records. On 24.11.76 original case records were put up and the learned Magistrate, after scrutinizing the final reports and the complaint petitions filed earlier held that there was no sufficient ground to proceed with the case and the same was dismissed by him. Being aggrieved the complainant preferred a revisional application against the order of dismissal passed on 24.11.76 before the learned Sessions Judge, Jessore who as per his order dated 18.3.78 passed an order for further enquiry into the matter. Being dissatisfied with the said order of the Sessions Judge, Jessore directing further enquiry, petitioners filed this application under section 435 and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and obtained this Rule. 3. Mr. Serajul Hoque, the learned Advocate has appeared on behalf of the petitioners. He submits that the order of the learned Sessions Judge is wholly illegal as he passed an order of further enquiry into the matter although the complaint petition was dismissed by the Magistrate He further submits that the order of enquiry made by the Sessions Judge, in the facts and circumstances of the case passed on misconception under the scope of section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. In support of his contention he has relied on a decision of the Supreme Court reported in 14 D. L. R. (S. C) page 96. Relying on this decision Mr. Serajul Hoque, the learned Advocate submits that the order of fresh enquiry as passed by the Sessions Judge was not warranted. According to him the order of dismissal passed by the learned Magistrate dismissing the com-plaint had the effect of acquittal; as such no further enquiry ought to have been ordered by the Sessions Judge. 

 6. It appears that an application was made before the then Prime Minister of Bangladesh on 3-5-73 alleging that four per-sons were kidnapped by the petitioners on 13-1-73 from Sabuj Sanga Club and another person was taken on the next day for interpretation and thereafter they were taken to a bil where they were killed by gun fire and thereafter their dead bodies were thrown into the Esamati bil. One of the deceased was a son of the complainant Rustom Ali. It appears that the police submitted a final report on 12-2-74 whereupon the accused persons were discharged against which a naraji petition was filed by the complainant on 29-3-74 before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate, Magura who sent the said petition to the Officer-in-Charge Mohammadpur for enquiry and report and thereafter it appears that another complaint petition was filed on 14-5-74 before the Magistrate about the same incident who sent the same to another Magistrate for holding Judicial enquiry. It further appears that on 30.5.74 and 6.6.74 the complainant remained absent before the Magistrate who was holding Judicial enquiry. As a result the learned Magistrate ordered the case to be flied: Thereafter the complainant filed a revival application for judicial enquiry and the same was revived and three witnesses were examined on 1.7.74 and adjourned to 4.11.74 for examination of further witnesses. In the meantime the complainant filed a petition before the magistrate stating that he was not willing to continue the proceeding as the witnesses were not willing to depose in the case. Whereupon the Judicial enquiry was dropped. On 24.6.76 the complainant filed another petition of complaint before the Sub-Divisional Magistrate Magura and the complainant was examined on oath and the said matter remained pending for about 5 months till 24.11.76 as the original records were not traced out. On 24.11.76 when the original records were traced out the learned Magistrate on consideration of the final report and the petition, dimissed the petition of complaint as per his order dated 26.11,76. As against that the complainant filed a revisional application before the Sessions Judge who as per his order dated 18.3.76 passed an order for further enquiry. As against that order the petitioners have filed this petition under section 435 and 439 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. From the annexures it appears that the petitioners along with others are of dangerous type of persons and due to this the complainant could not lodge the F.I.R. in time. Ultimately the complainant filed a petition before the then Prime Minister who directed the officer-in charge Mohammadpur to treat the same as F.I.R, It further appears that the petition which was filed before the Magistrate whereupon a Judicial enquiry was ordered was withdrawn by the complainant due to threat given to him by the petitioners. Be that as it may, it appears that the learned Sessions Judge considered all these aspects and directed fresh enquiry as per his order dated 18.3.78. In this connection we may refer to the provisions of section 436 of the Code of Criminal procedure which is as follows:- 

 "436. On examining any record under section 435 or otherwise, the High Court or the Sessions Judge may direct the District magistrate by himself or by any of the Magistrate subordinate to him to make, and the District Magistrate may himself make, or direct any Subordinate Magistrate to make; further enquiry into any complaint which has been dismissed under section 203 or sub-section (3) of section 204, or into the case of any person accused of an offence who has been discharged. Provided that no Court shall make any direction under this section for enquiry into the case of any person who has been discharged unless such person has had an opportunity of showing cause why such direction should not be made." 

 7. From the above provision it is clear that if the Sessions Judge on examining any record under section 435 or otherwise, the Sessions Judge may direct the District Magistrate or any other Magistrate subordinate to him to make, and the District Magistrate may himself make, or direct any Subordinate Magistrate to make further enquiry into any complaint which has been dismissed under section 203 or sub-section (3) of section 204, or into the case of any person accused of an offence who has been discharge. In the instant case it appears that the learned Sessions Judge acted in accordance with the pro-vision of section 436 as the complaint was dismissed by the learned magistrate and three persons were discharged. 

 8. In the case reported in 14 DLR page 96 in the case of Abul Hossain Sana Vs. Suwalal Agarwala and another wherein it was held by the Supreme Court of Pakistan: An express bar to fresh proceedings was not essential when the law provides for the exercise of jurisdiction Joy a Court the jurisdiction will be exhausted if it is exercised once. The jurisdiction which the court granted to the Magistrate by section 252 and 253, Criminal Procedure Code having been exhausted it is for him who invokes a power of revival to establish such power. In the absence of a specific provision the power shall be presumed not to exist. 

 10. In the presence of an order of acquittal fresh proceedings in respect of the same offence will be entirely without jurisdiction, while in the case of an order of discharge passed on the merits fresh proceedings will be improper and will not be permitted 

 11. In a proper case an application for revival may amount to a fresh complaint but barring that for the reasons already recorded a revival is not possible." 

 14. From the above decision it is further clear that whether the order of discharge has been passed on merits and on consideration of the materials on record in this case thus this decision will be applicable, but in the case where the order of dismissal is passed without considering the material on record, in that case this decision will be applicable. In the instant case the order of the Magistrate not being passed on consideration of evidence on record or on materials I hold that the learned Sessions Judge was justified hi passing the order of fresh inquiry under section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. 

 15. In this connection we may refer to the decision reported in 22 D.L.R. page 199 in the case of Md. Mostafa Chowdhury Vs. Lila Rani Naundi wherein this court held "Discharge order not based on merits. No bar to take cognizance of the same offence upon complaint. Magistrate passed an order of discharge of a case on account of the absence of the parties and without going into the merits of the case". 

 17. Mr. Syed Ghulam Mostafa, the learned Advocate has relied on a decision re-ported in 29. D.L.R. page 338 in the case of Habibullah Chowdhury-Vs Abdul Rader Howlader where it was held" an order of discharge is not passed upon any finding on the merits which of the charge against the accused will not stand in the way of taking cognizance upon fresh complaint." 

 18. It had been further held "that an order of discharge of a case on account of the parties and without going into the merits of the case is not a final order exhausting the power of the Magistrate and making him functus officio. Such an order is no bar in taking cognizance of an offence upon fresh complains." 

 19. From the above decision also it app-ears that an order of discharge which is not passed on merits on consideration of the evidence on record would not stand in the way of taking cognizance upon fresh complaint. It further appears that when the order by the Magistrate is not on merit it cannot be said that the order is final order exhausting the power of the Magistrate and making him functus officio. But in the facts and circumstances of the present case the order passed by the Magistrate cannot be said to be a final order as he has passed the order on consideration of merits. 

 20. Mr. Syed Ghulam Mostafa, the learned Advocate also relied on 25 D.L.R. page 152 in the case of Kanchan Ali Howlader-Vs-Abdul Malek and others wherein it was held: "Further enquiry under section 436 of the Cr. P.C. does not necessarily mean the taking of additional evidence but it may also mean reconsideration of the evidence already taken. 

 21. The term "further enquiry" in its wider meaning includes re-consideration of the evidence already on record as wail, and in some cases it means a new enquiry altogether by a different Magistrate. What step will be taken in a particular case will depend upon the circumstances of that case. 

 22. In this case the Sessions Judge who had ordered further enquiry did not give any specific direction as to which of these courses the Magistrate would adopt. It was therefore open to the Magistrate to take any of the steps indicated above, as facts of the case demanded." 

 23. Mr. Md. Serajul Hoque also relied on 30 DLR. page 344 and submits that the Sessions Judge cannot revive a case which has been finally decided by the Magistrate. According to Mr. Serajul Hoque the order of discharge against his client passed on consideration of the materials on record is the order of acquittal, in these circumstances the learned Sessions Judge ought not to have interfered with the order passed by the Magistrate and passed an order for further enquiry. I have considered the submission made by the learned Advocates and I am of the opinion that the learned Sessions Judge was perfectly justified in setting aside the order passed by the Magistrate and directing the Magistrate to proceed further with the case in accordance with law.
